title: Growing food in cities

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some consider that cities are at the forefront of future food solutions. There is an overall consensus that a lot of urban challenges can be addressed through policies linked to urban systems of food provisioning. Considering cities are increasingly stepping into the foreground as important actors in the advancement of resilient urban food systems (UFS), it is urgent that the many solutions being advanced throughout the world are shared. This is exactly what the book Cities and Agriculture, edited by Henk de Zeeuw and Pay Drechsel, accomplishes. The book is a collection of studies, written by a range of European academics. According to their areas of speciality, these contributors address different aspects of global food security and the role that cities have to play in achieving this, Global food security was defined in 1996 by the World Food Summit as "when all people at all times have access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food to maintain a healthy and active life'.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: As the populations of many cities expand, cities are grappling with a number of complex challenges, In the opening chapter of this book, Han Wiskerke notes that the most pressing challenges include governance and infrastructure; resource use; growing inequalities between rich and poor, environmental pollution; climate change; and most importantly, the continuing provision of food to urban centres. Wiskerke argues that by focusing on food provisioning, many of the other challenges can also number of complex challenges, In the opening chapter of this book, Han Wiskerke notes that the most pressing challenges include governance and infrastructure; resource use; growing inequalities between rich and poor, environmental pollution; climate change; and most importantly, the continuing provision of food to urban centres. Wiskerke argues that by focusing on food provisioning, many of the other challenges can also be addressed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The book highlights four key conditions that impact directly on UFS. The first condition involves population growth, urbanization, and changing diets. All of these put pressure on food security in terms of the affordability, adequacy, and availability of food resources, especially for the urban poor. In chapter five, Paule Moustier and Henk Renting show, through examples from Africa, Asia, and Latin America, where urban agriculture has always been a feature of many of their cities, that due to the proximity of the producer to the buyers, urban agriculture gives buyers direct access to information about quality, and delivers lower prices and fresher products.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Scarcity and depletion of resources are put forward as the second condition shaping UFS. The provision of food relies heavily on resources, such as fossil fuels, water, and land, However, as growing urban populations also produce more urban waste, there are ample opportunities for cities to extract resources from human and animal waste, and by doing so reduce cities' demands on primary resources. In chapter seven, Drechsel explores opportunities for the safe use of organic waste, as well as waste water, in urban agriculture, He emphasizes that there are a number of challenges related to health risks in the valorization" of waste water streams. However, he notes that, especially in cases of water scarcity, techniques to treat waste water are promising.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Thirdly, climate change has substantially impacted agricultural production worldwide as well as living conditions, especially in cities, in terms of access to fresh and varied food. According to Shuaib Lwasa and Marielle Dubbeling (chapter eight), when it comes to the adaptation to climate change, urban agriculture has the potential to contribute to the diversification of the food available and offer a source of income for urban dwellers. They add that agricultural areas within cities can also help to reduce the heat island effect (the term used to describe the fact that cities are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas) and the impact of natural disasters such as flooding.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Finally, public health and diet-related ill health correlate directly with urban food supply as obesity and malnutrition are increasingly issues with which cities are coping. This is very much connected to urbanization and changing diets, as a transition is taking place from a rural to an urban diet based more on animal proteins and processed foods. Maria Gerster-Bentaya argues in chapter six that food security for the urban poor is tightly tied to their livelihood, considering the majority of them must buy their food but often don't have sufficient income to buy all they need. Although certain health risks are connected to food produced in cities from toxins accumulating in urban produce through contaminated soil, to food safety concerns with street food - urban agriculture, nonetheless, improves access to food for the urban poor. Arguably, this also makes a more resilient urban food system, as consumers are less dependent upon international prices.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The book also offers detailed insights into different forms of urban agriculture, Urban animal farming is addressed and it is shown that it is a much-practiced form of urban agriculture in some less developed countries or regions as it is a good source of revenue and has the added bonus of shortening temperature-controlled sections in the supply chain that are needed for fresh products, Urban agro-forestry is dealt with and the argument made that there is a requirement to assess both the challenges and possible benefits that agro-forestry can provide in terms of ecosystem services, Overall, Cities and Agriculture offers a very comprehensive overview of urban agriculture, The information is relevant to researchers and policy-makers, and illustrates how these different groups can contribute to more resilient UFS.
